records.name_note: RHS's own database is internally split on this exact plant. Its species page for the plain binomial "Tulipa gesneriana" is flagged "Name Status: Synonym," while a separate RHS species page for "Tulipa × gesneriana" (the hybrid-marked name, reflecting that garden tulips are of hybrid breeding origin) is flagged "Name Status: Correct." The cultivation, hardiness, and hazard data are identical between the two pages — only the name status differs. No other admissible source in this record's source list (NC State, Clemson, Missouri Botanical Garden, UF/IFAS, Penn State, Maryland, UGA) addresses this taxonomic point to corroborate or contradict RHS's own resolution, so RHS's designation is used as given: scientific_name_accepted is set to "Tulipa × gesneriana."

fertilize_interval_days — removed on audit: The cited RHS growing-guide page conditions the weekly-feeding advice: 'If you grow tulips as bedding (disposed of the bulbs after they've finished flowering) there is no need to feed bulbs,' and separately explains 'Border tulips often fail to flower in their second year when left in the ground. For this reason they are often treated as seasonal colour (bedding) and disposed of after flowering.' That is exactly the practice the record's own is_houseplant citation (Clemson) documents as typical -- tulips 'treated like annual flowers, dug and discarded after they have bloomed.' The record states fertilize_interval_days=7 as an unqualified general value, omitting the source's own caveat that for the very use-case its own other citation calls typical, no feeding is needed at all. Secondarily, '7' is not literally present in the quote -- 'weekly' is a word, not the numeral -- which fails the record's own literal-number-derivation standard (the only carved-out exception is month-name conversion for fertilize_active_months, which doesn't apply here).

is_houseplant — removed on audit: The sole citation (Clemson) supports only that South Carolina gardeners treat tulips as single-season, dug-and-discarded bedding plants -- it never addresses indoor cultivation or houseplant status one way or the other. No admissible source in the record addresses whether tulips are or aren't grown as houseplants (e.g., the well-known practice of forcing tulip bulbs to bloom indoors in pots is never mentioned). The record conflates 'grown outdoors and replaced annually' with 'not a houseplant' -- two different axes the citation doesn't actually bridge.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The phrase 'All parts are harmful if eaten' overstates the RHS quote, which is an unqualified 'Harmful if eaten; skin allergen' that never specifies 'all parts.' This sits in tension with the same field's own Penn State-sourced statement that the bulb carries 'by far' the highest toxin concentration of any part -- a distribution that undercuts, rather than supports, a claim that literally all parts are (implicitly equally) harmful. The core toxic-if-eaten / bulb-risk conclusion is well sourced; the 'All parts' framing specifically is not literally stated by any cited source and should be softened (e.g. to 'the plant').

cool_rest_note — removed on audit: The 12-14 week / 33-40F figures come from University of Maryland Extension's guide to commercial greenhouse cut-flower forcing production, not general garden-bed cultivation. The record's own unknowns section acknowledges this same UMD document's temperature data describes 'a commercial forcing/storage technique for controlling bloom timing in cut-flower production' and explicitly excludes it from day_f/night_f fields on that basis -- yet cool_rest_note uses the same document's same-context storage figure as if it were general garden-bulb chilling guidance. This is an inconsistent application of the record's own exclusion principle and risks telling a home gardener their in-ground bulbs need 12-14 weeks of active refrigeration, when Clemson (the properly garden-context source) is the only citation actually describing home-garden bulb-chilling practice.

records.name_note: No conflict among admissible sources on the accepted binomial. NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox page for this species lists "Euphorbia coccinea" and "Poinsettia pulcherrima" under a "Previously known as:" heading, confirming Euphorbia pulcherrima is the currently accepted name and those two are historical synonyms, not competing accepted names.
records.toxicity_detail: Its reputation as seriously poisonous is exaggerated. Penn State Extension (in an article specifically about holiday plants and pets) says the milky, latex-like sap "can irritate pets' stomachs, but gastrointestinal upset symptoms should resolve on their own" — i.e. a mild, self-limiting GI irritant, not a severe toxin. NC State Extension separately tags the species "Problem for Cats," "Problem for Dogs," and "Problem for Horses," corroborating that pets are flagged as affected, though NC State does not give pet-specific symptom detail — its detailed "Poison Severity: Low" / contact-dermatitis symptom data is filed specifically under a human-focused "Poisonous to Humans" section on that same page and was deliberately not imported into this pet-toxicity assessment.
records.cool_rest_note: If kept past the holidays, reduce water after bloom and let the plant go dormant, moving it to a cooler spot that still stays above 50°F, then resume fertilizing once spring arrives.
records.water_dry_down_target: Water when the soil/potting-mix surface feels dry to the touch; never let it dry out completely and never let the pot sit in standing water.

UMD states only an imprecise 'mid-fifties overnight'; Clemson's '55 to 60 °F' figure is given as the point at which an outdoor-grown potted plant should be brought back indoors (a protective threshold), not a stated ideal night range; NC State's 'night temperatures in the low 60s' is specifically the trigger needed to force bract color for the next Christmas, a different, rebloom-specific claim.

day_f_min/day_f_max (60/70) reflects the cluster shared by UMD, Clemson, RHS, and NC State. UF/IFAS EP349 states a notably higher 'temperature range of 65°F (night) and 75°F–80°F (day)' with no overlap against the 60-70 day range the other four sources describe; treated as an outlier and not used, possibly reflecting a tropical/Florida-landscape framing rather than the indoor-holiday-plant comfort range the other sources give.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The record's only citation for the accepted name is RHS's 'C. x limon is an ancient hybrid, derived from several wild species' -- but a direct fetch of the UF/IFAS HS402 page (a lemon-dedicated publication, also cited elsewhere in this record) shows it gives the scientific name as 'Citrus limon Burm. f.' -- a full binomial WITH a taxonomic authority citation (Burman filius) and NO hybrid marker at all, not even an informal 'x'. That is not a stylistic '×' vs 'x' difference as the record claims -- it is UF/IFAS treating the plant as a settled species with a named authority, versus RHS treating it as an unstable ancient hybrid with no authority citation given. That is a real disagreement about accepted taxonomic status, and picking RHS's framing as 'accepted' without reconciling the UF/IFAS binomial is over-reach. Per the audit's rule (structural check 4), this should either be left null or the conflict documented honestly, not resolved by fiat.

name_note — removed on audit: name_note asserts 'NC State, UF/IFAS, and Missouri Botanical Garden write it as "Citrus x limon" or "Citrus limon" without the formal symbol... there is no accepted-name conflict, only a notation difference.' This is false for UF/IFAS specifically: its scientific-name line reads 'Citrus limon Burm. f.' -- a full authority-cited species name, not 'Citrus x limon' minus a symbol. The note flattens a genuine taxonomic-treatment disagreement (hybrid-with-no-authority vs. species-with-authority) into a cosmetic one, which misleads a reader relying on this field.

humidity_need — removed on audit: The only support is one Clemson 'Container Citrus Production' sentence: 'At least 8 hours of sunlight and high humidity, 30% to 60%, are required for optimum growth and development.' That sentence is generic guidance for citrus grown in containers under Clemson's system -- it doesn't name lemon or single out a cultivar. The citation's own justification for relevance ('mentions C. limon cultivars Eureka and Meyer by name') is itself inaccurate: Eureka is a true lemon cultivar, but Meyer lemon is Citrus × meyeri, a distinct hybrid, not a Citrus limon cultivar -- so the page's scope spans more than just true lemon, and the humidity line is not shown to be lemon-specific.

humidity_pct_min — removed on audit: Same defect as humidity_need: this number rests solely on the same genus/multi-cultivar Clemson container-citrus sentence, whose species-specificity claim (via the 'Eureka and Meyer' justification) is undermined by Meyer lemon actually being a different species (Citrus × meyeri), not a C. limon cultivar.

humidity_pct_max — removed on audit: Same defect as humidity_need/humidity_pct_min: sole support is the generic Clemson container-citrus humidity line, not shown to be specific to true lemon rather than the broader mix of citrus/cultivars the factsheet covers.

direct_sun_hours_max — removed on audit: Sourced from UMD's 'Growing Dwarf Citrus': 'place your citrus tree outdoors to receive... 8 to 12 hours of direct sun exposure.' This is the exact same genus-broad 'citrus tree' phrasing (from the exact same UMD guide, which the record's own unknowns entry says covers 'dwarf lemons/limes/mandarins/kumquats... not isolated to lemon specifically') that the record correctly used to justify leaving day_f_min/max and night_f_min/max null. The record applied the genus-generality exclusion rule to the temperature fields but not to this structurally identical sun-hours sentence from the same source, letting a genus-level number stand in as lemon's specific value.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The sole citation's quote is 'Soil Drainage: Good Drainage, Moist' (confirmed verbatim on the live NC State page). That describes good/well-drained soil, not 'moderate' drainage -- the record asserts a category the quote doesn't literally support, the same failure mode the audit brief itself warns about (e.g. 'part_shade' asserted from a 'light shade' quote). 'Good Drainage' and 'moderate drainage' are not the same claim.

chill_damage_f — removed on audit: UF/IFAS's quote gives four distinct freeze-damage thresholds for lemon, not one: defoliation at 22-24°F, severe wood damage at 20°F, flower/young-fruit kill at 29°F, and mature-fruit damage at 28-31°F. The record picked the defoliation figure (24°F) as the general chill_damage_f value, but the source's own data shows fruit and flower damage begin at a WARMER temperature (28-31°F) than leaf defoliation -- meaning real cold injury to this tree starts well before 24°F is reached. If chill_damage_f is meant to represent the point at which the plant first sustains cold damage (as its generic field name suggests, rather than a field specifically scoped to defoliation), the record's choice understates the risk by roughly 4-7°F, and the citation doesn't explain why defoliation rather than the earlier flower/fruit thresholds was chosen as representative.

normalizations: 2026-08-22: second batch of the "blind spots" pass -- common garden and houseplant staples that were, oddly, never in the original 129-species curated catalog: rose, tulip, daffodil, poinsettia, cyclamen, Spanish moss (air plant), lemon tree, and periwinkle. Poinsettia and cyclamen carry real mild-to-moderate toxicity that popular myth often gets wrong in both directions; tulip and daffodil bulbs are a documented dog-digs-up-and-chews hazard distinct from the flowers/leaves.

This batch's verify prompt was rewritten after b19 exposed a real bug: the landing script nulled an entire field whenever any single finding on it was refuted, even when the value was independently supported by other, unflagged citations. The rewrite told the auditor to distinguish a citation-level defect from a value-level one and only refute the field when the value itself is in doubt. It worked -- every one of the 15 fields removed in this batch is a genuine value-level defect (a category the quote doesn't literally support, a genus-level figure presented as species-specific, human-toxicity content bleeding into a pet field, or an internal contradiction the record didn't surface), not an over-broad null over one bad citation among several good ones.

One cosmetic fix at landing: Tulip's common_name was nulled because the record wrote "Garden Tulip," dropping "common" from RHS's exact listed name ("common garden tulip, late tulip") -- restored using the source's literal wording rather than left null, since the underlying fact was never in question.

Two genuinely toxic, commonly pet-accessible species -- Vinca minor (periwinkle) and Rosa rugosa -- correctly landed with toxic_to_pets null rather than guessed: the only admissible toxicity source found for periwinkle (UGA) is explicitly scoped to human toxicity, and no admissible source addresses rugosa rose at all. Left as honest gaps rather than repaired, since general veterinary-toxicology knowledge of Vinca alkaloids isn't an admissible extension-service citation.
